endorsements.quote: Therefore, clinicians must treat AI‐based devices like any other medical device and ensure their use is consistent with the intended purpose it was approved for.

In Australia, any AI‐based application that otherwise fulfills the role of a medical device and has not received regulatory approval for its intended use cannot be used in clinical care unless it is exempt from regulation.

unlisted_practices: Surgeons should demand transparency about data handling from AI software vendors.
Surgeons should use vendors that do not return patient data for algorithm training.
Professional bodies such as colleges should support clinicians in acquiring AI privacy knowledge through Continuous Professional Development platforms.
Clinicians should understand whether the training sample of an AI tool represents the patient population to which it is applied.
Ethics committees reviewing AI-based trials should have extended expertise in data governance, supported by NHMRC guidance.
Educational bodies should develop governance strategies to authenticate authorship of AI-assisted research.

screen.reason: The article is a commentary/framework introducing a traffic light coding system for surgical engagement with AI, offering guidance and principles rather than empirical evaluation.
